document.title: Protest of the Solar Energy Industries Association and Advanced Energy United
document.group: MISO Large Load Addition Resource Study (LARS)

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, 
Inc. 
) 
) 
) 
 
Docket No. ER27-25-000 
 
PROTEST OF THE SOLAR ENERGY INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION  
AND ADVANCED ENERGY UNITED 
 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (Commission) 
Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA)2 and 
Advanced Energy United (United)3 submit this protest of the Midcontinent Independent System 
Operator, Inc.’s (MISO) LARS filing.4  
In the LARS filing, MISO proposes a process that would study load and generation on a 
coordinated basis. But to enter that process, a load and generation owner must be granted access 
by the Transmission Customer, which in MISO, is also often a vertically integrated Load Serving 
Entity (LSE) and Transmission Owner (TO).5 In this way, a Transmission Customer is also a 
direct competitor to independent power producers in developing generation in MISO. MISO 
proposes to effectively grant the Transmission Customer, which has an incentive to discriminate 
against competitive generation, the ability to discriminate against competitive generation. By 
 
1 18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2026). 
2 The comments contained in this filing represent the position of SEIA as a trade organization on behalf of the solar 
industry, but do not necessarily reflect the views of any particular member with respect to any issue. 
3  Advanced Energy United is a national association of businesses that are making the energy we use secure, clean 
and affordable. Advanced Energy United is the only industry association in the United States that represents the full 
range of advanced energy technologies and services, both grid-scale and distributed. Advanced energy includes 
energy efficiency, demand response, energy storage, wind, solar, hydro, nuclear, electric vehicles, and more. The 
comments expressed in this filing represent the position of Advanced Energy United but may not represent the views 
of any particular member with respect to any issue. 
4 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., LARS, Docket No. ER26-3813-000 (Sept. 21, 2026) (LARS 
Proposal). 
5See Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 170 FERC ¶ 61,215, P 13 (2020) (“Notably, approximately 90% of the 
load in MISO is served by vertically integrated LSEs…”); see also Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 191 
FERC ¶ 61,131, P 87 (2025) (ERAS 1.0 Order); and Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 189 FERC ¶ 61,159, 
PP 6, 27 (2024).

2 
vesting the Transmission Customer with the discretion to file the LARS application,6 MISO turns 
what could have been a just and reasonable process into one that is unjust, unreasonable, and 
unduly discriminatory.  
MISO could have filed a proposal that worked for many stakeholders, rather than just a 
few; MISO still can make such a proposal. SEIA and United respectfully request that the 
Commission reject the LARS proposal, on the grounds that the proposal is unduly 
discriminatory, and provide guidance to MISO to refile the proposal with a mechanism that 
would allow any qualified market participant—including independent power producers, 
developers, and load customers—to initiate a submission, provided the applicable readiness and 
securitization requirements are met. However, if the Commission accepts LARS, SEIA and 
United request that the Commission expressly clarify that the Associated Transmission 
Customer’s exclusive application role must be executed in a nondiscriminatory manner. 
 
I. 
PROTEST 
A. The LARS Proposal is unduly discriminatory because it allows LSEs to 
decide if their competitors may participate in the LARS process. 
 
MISO’s filing is part of its efforts to comply with the Commission’s June 18, 2026, Show 
Cause Order.7 As relevant here, the Show Cause Order found that MISO’s tariff may be unjust 
and unreasonable because it does not contain provisions allowing an interconnection customer to 
seek interconnection service that reflects the operational dynamics of serving electrically 
proximate load.8 
 
6 Transmittal at 6, 24. 
7 Transmittal at 3. 
8 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal 
Power Act, 195 FERC ¶ 61,212 at P 113 (2026) (“Show Cause Order”).

3 
Under the LARS Proposal, MISO would study load and generation pairs in parallel, with 
both study processes brought under a common application.9 To be eligible for LARS, an 
Interconnection Customer and the LARS Associated Load must provide an agreement 
demonstrating that the output of the LARS Generating Facility will serve the LARS Associated 
Load.10 This agreement, along with the other LARS requirements, would be part of the LARS 
Application submitted by the LARS Associated Transmission Customer,11 which is the “entity 
that procures Transmission Service for load and has a direct relationship with the load,” and 
“often a Load Serving Entity (“LSE”).”12 The LARS Associated Transmission Customer is the 
only party that may initiate the LARS Application.13 
As MISO states, the LARS Associated Transmission Customer is often a Load Serving 
Entity,14 and in the MISO region, LSE are often vertically integrated utilities that have a 
generation affiliate and/or build their own generation.15 These entities have a competitive motive 
to discriminate in favor of their own facilities.16 Utility-owned generators are competing with 
independent power producers for the ability to be the power procurement solution for new large 
loads in MISO. MISO’s proposed LARS creates a process wherein that competition to serve a 
new LARS Associated Load is organized and refereed by one of the competitors – the 
Transmission Customer utility. The Transmission Customer is the utility party with an interest in 
 
9 Transmittal at 5. 
10 Transmittal at 9. 
11 Transmittal at 7. 
12 Transmittal at 6. 
13 Transmittal at 6. 
14 Transmittal at 6. 
15 See Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 170 FERC ¶ 61,215, P 13 (2020) (“Notably, approximately 90% of 
the load in MISO is served by vertically integrated LSEs…”); see also Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 191 
FERC ¶ 61,131, P 87 (2025) (ERAS 1.0 Order); and Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 189 FERC ¶ 61,159, 
PP 6, 27 (2024). 
16 Am. Clean Power Ass'n v. FERC, 54 F.4th 722, 728 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (discussing Ameren Servs. Co. v. FERC, 880 
F.3d 571, 578 (D.C. Cir. 2018)).

4 
prioritizing its own generation development and limiting competition from independently 
developed generation within its service territory. Moreover, the Transmission Customer is often 
the same utility that owns the existing transmission infrastructure and is responsible for 
constructing the additional transmission facilities needed to accommodate the interconnection 
customer’s generation and associated load. This is antithetical to the very purpose of Order No. 
2003. 
In Order No. 2003, the Commission found that “public utilities owning or controlling 
jurisdictional transmission facilities had the incentive to engage in, and had engaged in, unduly 
discriminatory transmission practices.”17 Because interconnection is an element of transmission 
service, the Commission established standard terms and procedures to “remedy undue 
discrimination and preferences under Sections 205 and 206 of the Federal Power Act.”18 The 
Commission did state that it would allow Regional Transmission Organizations and Independent 
System Operators (RTOs/ISOs), such as MISO, to propose independent entity variations for 
pricing and non-pricing provisions.19 The Commission granted RTOs this flexibility because an 
RTO “is less likely to act in an unduly discriminatory manner than a Transmission Provider that 
is a market participant.”20 Despite this being a process under the MISO Tariff, MISO designed 
LARS to ensure it is the Transmission Customer—who has the incentive to discriminate against 
competitors—that controls access to the LARS process. 
Critical to any decision on MISO’s proposed LARS process is the understanding that 
MISO’s use of the Transmission Customer, while sensible because the Transmission Customer 
 
17 Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements & Procs., Order No. 2003, 104 FERC ¶ 61,103, P 13 
(2003). 
18 Id. at P 19. 
19 Id. at P 827. 
20 Id.

5 
procures transmission service for load interconnecting to MISO’s system, is in practical effect 
the same as MISO saying the vertically integrated LSE/TO utility; when a LARS Interconnection 
Request is in that utility’s footprint, is in charge of whether to move a LARS project forward. 
That result presents the very instance the Commission adopted Order No. 2003 to address: 
“when the Transmission Provider is not independent and has an interest in frustrating rival 
generators.”21 MISO’s flexibility to depart from the pro forma LGIP under the independent entity 
variation standard rests on the Commission’s premise that an RTO or ISO is “less likely to act in 
an unduly discriminatory manner than a Transmission Provider that is a market participant.”22 
That premise does not support LARS when the decision whether any generator enters the process 
is handed to the market participant whose own generation the interconnection customer would be 
competing against. 
MISO claims that independent power producers are not prohibited from participating in 
the LARS process.23 MISO is right. There is nothing in the Tariff language that expressly 
prohibits independent power producers from participating in the LARS process. However, 
simply stating that the process is open does not actually make the process meaningfully open. 
Yes, independent power producers can participate in the LARS process—if their competitors 
will let them.  
Just as there is no express prohibition on independent power producer participation in 
LARS, there is no express requirement that a LARS Associated Transmission Customer must 
submit a request. Under the proposed tariff, it is possible for the LARS Associated Transmission 
Customer to hold up an otherwise viable arrangement between an independent Interconnection 
 
21 Id. at P 696. 
22 Id. at P 827. 
23 Transmittal at 7-8.

6 
Customer and a LARS Associated Load. An independent power producer may have an executed 
agreement with the large-load customer, substantial site control, and a commercially mature 
project, but will remain unable to submit into the LARS process without signoff from the 
Transmission Customer.  
The proposal requires the Transmission Owner—which again in MISO is likely to also be 
the LARS Associated Transmission Customer—to meet with the LARS Interconnection 
Customer and any other impacted parties.24 However, there is enough ambiguity in the tariff to 
allow the Transmission Owner/ LARS Associated Transmission Customer to slow down a 
request. The tariff states that the parties “shall jointly agree upon a feasible Point of 
Interconnection” no later than 10 days before the LARS Application deadline.25 But, there is no 
provisions for situations in which the parties cannot agree on the Point of Interconnection, and 
there is no mechanism by which the LARS Interconnection Customer can seek recourse if the 
parties do not agree on a Point of Interconnection. Nor are there any provisions that require the 
LARS Associated Transmission Customer to submit an application, effectively granting them the 
ability to prevent independent power producers from entering the LARS process. 
This undue discrimination can be fixed. SEIA and United request that the Commission 
reject MISO’s LARS proposal, because it is unduly discriminatory. SEIA and United also 
request that the Commission provide guidance to MISO to refile the proposal with a mechanism 
that would allow any qualified market participant—including independent power producers, 
developers, and load customers—to initiate a submission directly to MISO, provided the 
applicable readiness and securitization requirements are met. 
 
24 Proposed Tariff, Attach. X, Sec. 3.12.1. 
25 Proposed Tariff, Attach. X, Sec. 3.12.1.

7 
B. The LARS proposal is unjust and unreasonable because it conditions 
generators’ interconnection rights on specific large loads while risking double-
counted transmission headroom, harm to earlier-queued projects, and 
improper cost shifts. 
i. LARS makes a generator’s rights depend on a specific large load, 
exposing viable projects to operational and financial uncertainty if 
that load departs. 
MISO’s proposed LARS framework provides expedited Interconnection Service based on 
a generator’s relationship with a particular large load,26 but fails to address the very real 
possibility that the relationship may be altered over time due to business decisions of the large 
load, creating significant uncertainty regarding the long-term durability of a generator’s 
interconnection rights.27 Without any kind of transition mechanism, this uncertainty may force 
otherwise viable generating resources into an uncertain and potentially disruptive transition 
process. By transferring the risk of the load customer’s future business decisions to the generator, 
the proposal could penalize generators for circumstances they cannot control and thereby deter 
otherwise viable projects from using the LARS pathway. 
Under the LARS Proposal, a generator’s eligibility for LARS Interconnection Service is 
tied to the continued existence of a specific associated large load for a substantial portion of the 
generator’s operating life.28 LARS provides off-ramps when an associated load departs.29 If the 
LARS Associated Load withdraws, ceases taking transmission service, or the required 
commercial agreement terminates during the first fifteen years, the generator’s LLGIA ultimately 
will be terminated and the generator must obtain new Interconnection Service through the 
Definitive Planning Process (DPP) to continue operating.30 This proposed structure creates a 
 
26 Transmittal at 7. 
27 Transmittal at 16. 
28 Transmittal at 5. 
29 Transmittal at 34. 
30 Transmittal at 16-18.

8 
material risk that a generator could lose the benefit of its expedited interconnection path through 
no fault of its own. Large-load facilities may cease operations, relocate, reduce demand, change 
suppliers, or otherwise alter their commercial arrangements for reasons unrelated to the 
generator’s performance. When this occurs, the generator faces uncertainty regarding its future 
operating rights and potential migration into the DPP process.31  
MISO acknowledges that the proposed process could “strand a Generating Facility” with 
remaining useful life and create “significant long-term commercial risk” affecting project 
financing,32 yet its proposed structure does not resolve those concerns. The risk of stranding a 
generator is particularly acute given the long development timelines and financing horizons of 
generation projects. Developers, lenders, and investors require predictable, durable 
interconnection rights. Conditioning those rights on the continuation of a particular customer 
relationship introduces uncertainty that may undermine financing and increase project costs. In 
effect, the proposal requires developers to evaluate not only the viability of the generation 
project, but also the associated load’s long-term business prospects. 
The proposed transition mechanism is woefully inadequate to address this stranded asset 
risk. If an associated load departs during the period in which the generator remains subject to the 
fifteen-year pairing requirement, the generator’s LLGIA ultimately may be terminated and the 
generator must obtain new Interconnection Service through the DPP to continue operations.33 
MISO proposes only a temporary transition period of up to one year, during which the generating 
facility would remain subject to Quarterly Operating Limits (QOL) and Annual ERIS (AERIS) 
restrictions while seeking new Interconnection Service through the DPP.34 Although MISO states 
 
31 Transmittal at 16-18; 34-35; 41-42. 
32 Transmittal at 17. 
33 Transmittal at 34. 
34 Transmittal at 17, 35.

9 
that it expects future DPP cycles will be completed within one year and provides for an extension 
if DPP processing is delayed beyond the generator's control,35 MISO provides little support for 
that assumption and does not demonstrate that a generator can transition to the DPP without 
adverse operational or commercial impacts.36 Given the current backlogged status of the DPP, 
the possibility of being put through that process means exposure to potentially years of delay, 
even after a facility has already entered commercial operation. 
MISO’s limited transition stands in stark contrast to the approach taken by the Southwest 
Power Pool (SPP) in its High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (HILLGA) proposal, 
which the Commission specifically referenced as an example when directing other regions to 
ensure adequate pathways for studying electrically proximate load and generation together.37 In 
HILLGA, SPP establishes upfront that generators using the pathway are granted only Load 
Limited Resource Interconnection Service (LLRIS), and provides five years for the 
interconnecting generator to obtain full interconnection rights.38 While LARS differs from 
HILLGA in other important ways, the necessity of a clear pathway for the interconnecting 
generator to become a system resource applies equally here. 
Absent additional protections, MISO’s proposal creates the possibility of an arbitrary 
interconnection-service cliff in which a resource that was properly interconnected, financed, and 
operating becomes subject to substantial uncertainty because of events occurring outside the 
generator's control. Such outcomes would undermine investment certainty and could discourage 
participation in the very framework MISO seeks to establish. 
 
35 Transmittal at 18. 
36 Transmittal at 17-18, 35, 41-42. 
37 EL.26-70-000 at 14.  
38 ER26-247-000 Transmittal at 5.

10 
Accordingly, the Commission should reject the LARS filing, and direct MISO to provide 
additional clarity in a subsequent proposal regarding the treatment of generators when associated 
loads cease operations or otherwise terminate the relationship underlying a LARS request. MISO 
should establish transparent transition procedures, clearly define the rights and obligations of 
affected generators, and ensure that generators are not exposed to unreasonable operational or 
commercial risks due solely to changes in a customer’s circumstances. 
ii. MISO has not demonstrated how transmission capability will be 
transparently managed across parallel LARS and DPP study 
processes to protect earlier-queued projects from double-counted 
headroom, cost shifts, and diminished available capability. 
MISO has not adequately demonstrated that the proposed LARS framework will preserve 
transparency and certainty for customers currently progressing through the Generator 
Interconnection Queue. While MISO states that protecting the DPP process was an express 
consideration during development of the proposal,39 there is limited detail regarding how 
transmission capability assumptions will be coordinated between LARS and DPP studies or how 
potential conflicts will be identified and resolved before stakeholders make significant 
commercial and development decisions.40  
Under the proposal, LARS and DPP requests will be studied separately and using 
different assumptions.41 MISO specifically states that LARS studies will not include 
interconnection requests currently in the generator interconnection queue that have not executed 
GIAs.42 As a result, projects advancing through the two processes may be evaluated based on 
different assumptions regarding future system conditions and available transmission capability.43 
 
39 Transmittal at 20. 
40 Transmittal at 51. 
41 Transmittal at 23. 
42 Transmittal at 12. 
43 Transmittal at 12-13.

11 
 
MISO contends that the separate study frameworks ultimately will be reconciled through 
the MISO Transmission Expansion Plan (MTEP) process, and argues that LARS projects will 
not affect DPP studies because the projects are evaluated independently.44 Although LARS 
customers remain responsible for applicable Network Upgrade costs, cost responsibility is not 
the central concern. The filing does not adequately explain how MISO will coordinate 
transmission-capability assumptions across parallel interconnection processes. Nor does it 
explain how existing queue customers will receive timely visibility into contemporaneous LARS 
studies before making significant commercial and development decisions. These uncertainties 
could create unjust and unreasonable results for interconnection customers and must be clarified.  
Specifically, the filing does not sufficiently explain how reconciliation between the 
LARS and DPP processes will occur relative to key interconnection milestones, including 
completion of studies, execution of GIAs, commencement of construction activities, and major 
financing commitments. Although MISO states that reconciliation will occur through MTEP, the 
proposal provides little information regarding when potential conflicts between LARS and DPP 
assumptions will be identified or how affected customers will be informed.45  
This lack of transparency raises concerns irrespective of ultimate cost responsibility. 
Interconnection customers routinely make substantial commercial commitments based on study 
results and anticipated interconnection outcomes. Developers rely on those results when 
negotiating financing arrangements, equipment procurement contracts, power purchase 
agreements, and other project milestones. Yet the filing provides little explanation regarding how 
 
44 Transmittal at 13, 20. 
45 Transmittal at 13, 20.

12 
interconnection customers will be notified if assumptions underlying those commitments are 
later modified as a result of reconciliation between LARS and DPP studies.46  
Nor does MISO identify a clear mechanism for addressing circumstances in which 
transmission capability assumptions used in one process ultimately prove inconsistent with 
assumptions used in the other process. While MISO generally states that resulting transmission 
needs would be addressed through existing planning processes and cost-allocation mechanisms,47 
MISO does not explain when such inconsistencies would be identified, whether customers would 
receive advance notice of potential impacts, or how MISO would ensure that existing queue 
customers retain reasonable certainty regarding their interconnection expectations as the two 
processes operate concurrently.  MISO acknowledges that stakeholders specifically raised issues 
regarding the relationship between LARS and the existing Generator Interconnection Queue 
during the stakeholder process,48 but does not sufficiently resolve these issues. MISO’s proposal 
offers limited detail regarding the specific procedures that will preserve transparency and 
predictability for customers already progressing through the queue, creating uncertainty and 
discouraging participation. 
Accordingly, the Commission should require MISO to provide additional information 
regarding how transmission-capability assumptions will be coordinated between LARS and DPP 
studies, when reconciliation will occur relative to major interconnection milestones, how 
affected customers will be notified of resulting impacts, and what safeguards will ensure that 
existing queue customers maintain sufficient visibility into the transmission capability 
 
46 Transmittal at 20. 
47 Transmittal at 13. 
48 Transmittal at 20, 51.

13 
assumptions underlying parallel LARS studies before significant commercial commitments are 
made.  
 
III. 
ALTERNATIVE RECOMMENDATION 
A. Alternatively, the Commission should clarify that the LARS application 
process must be administered on a nondiscriminatory basis.   
 
If the Commission disagrees with SEIA and United that MISO’s LARS proposal is unjust 
and unreasonable, or unduly discriminatory, and accepts the proposal, SEIA and United request, 
in the alternative, that the Commission expressly clarify that the LARS Associated Transmission 
Customer’s exclusive initial application role does not authorize discriminatory treatment of an 
otherwise qualified applicant. As discussed above, the Federal Power Act and Order No. 2003 
require just and reasonable, nondiscriminatory access to jurisdictional transmission and generator 
interconnection service.49 To preserve those principles, the Commission should expressly require 
nondiscriminatory administration of LARS from the outset. 
Specifically, the Commission should clarify that once an applicant meets all applicable 
LARS eligibility, readiness, financial security, and application requirements, the Commission 
expects the LARS Associated Transmission Customer to apply the same submission standards 
and timelines it applies to its own similarly situated projects. During stakeholder engagement, 
MISO responded to concerns about limiting application submission to LSEs by explaining that 
IPPs could participate as Interconnection Customers, even though the Associated Transmission 
Customer would initiate the application.50 That response, however, does not resolve the concern 
 
49 16 U.S.C. § 824d(a)–(b); Order No. 2003, 104 FERC ¶ 61,103, PP 12, 18–20. 
50 MISO, MISO Response to Feedback: Large Load Addition Resource Study (LARS), at 6 (Aug. 20, 2026), 
https://cdn.misoenergy.org/LLWG%20Generation%20and%20Large%20Load%20Alignment%20Response%20%2
8LLWG-2026-6%29%20%2820260716%29778046.pdf (Feedback: “Why is the submittal limited to Load Serving 
Entities? This is potentially discriminatory to IPPs.” MISO Response: “While the LARS application process will be

14 
that the Associated Transmission Customer could use its control over submission to favor its 
own generation. The requested clarification would preserve the Associated Transmission 
Customer’s service role in the LARS process while ensuring nondiscriminatory access to the 
coordinated study process.  
The Commission should also expressly clarify that acceptance of LARS does not insulate 
discriminatory implementation from subsequent challenges. This would be consistent with the 
Commission’s adjudication of Section 206 complaints challenging interconnection study 
procedures. For example, in EDF Renewable Energy, Inc. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, 
Inc., the Commission permitted the RTOs to retain their existing Affected Systems modeling 
standards “assuming they apply such criteria and procedures consistently and on a not unduly 
discriminatory basis among all interconnection requests.”51 The Commission should likewise 
clarify that retaining the Associated Transmission Customer’s application role does not foreclose 
review of discriminatory administration of LARS upon a future, case-specific complaint. An 
express clarification would provide notice of the governing standard and strengthen the basis for 
case-specific relief while preserving MISO’s proposed application structure. 
 
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
MISO’s proposal makes the Transmission Customers—most often vertically integrated 
LSE and TO utility—the gatekeepers of this new competitively advantageous process. In a 
region such as MISO’s where many utilities are vertically integrated, that role grants these 
 
initiated by the LARS Associated Transmission Customer, the Interconnection Customer, Transmission Owner, and 
LARS Associated Transmission Customer must all complete the required information as part of the application 
before it will be reviewed by MISO. IPPs are not prohibited from participating as the Interconnection Customer as 
part of the process.”).  
51 EDF Renewable Energy, Inc. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 168 FERC ¶ 61,173, P 86 (2019).

15 
utilities the ability to determine which, if any, of its competitors may participate in the LARS 
process. And regardless of which projects go through the LARS process, the impact on earlier-
queued projects will be negative. While there are aspects of the filing that would pass muster 
under the Federal Power Act, its proposal to install the Transmission Customer as the 
gatekeepers to the LARS process and impacts to the existing queue are why it does not meet its 
burden under the Federal Power Act. SEIA and United request that the Commission reject 
MISO’s filing with guidance to MISO to refile the proposal with a mechanism that would allow 
any qualified market participant—including independent power producers, developers, and load 
customers—to initiate a submission directly to MISO, provided the applicable readiness and 
securitization requirements are met. Allowing LSEs to determine which of its competitors may 
participate in the markets would undermine Order No. 2003. However, if the Commission 
accepts MISO’s proposal, SEIA and United request that the Commission expressly clarify that 
the LARS application process must be administered on a nondiscriminatory basis and that 
acceptance does not foreclose subsequent challenges to discriminatory implementation. 
 
Respectfully submitted,
